items.title: Frontend Engineering at Palantir: Redefining Real-Time Map Collaboration
items.hover_description:
How we built lightweight, real-time map collaboration for teams operating at the edge.

About This Series

Frontend engineering at Palantir goes far beyond building standard web apps. Our engineers design interfaces for mission-critical decision-making, build operational applications that translate insight to action, and create systems that handle massive datasets — thinking not just about what the user needs, but what they need when the network is unreliable, the stakes are high, and the margin for error is zero.

This series pulls back the curtain on what that work really looks like: the technical problems we solve, the impact we have, and the approaches we take. Whether you’re just curious or exploring opportunities to join us, these posts offer an authentic look at life on our Frontend teams.

In this blog post, Leon, a Full Stack engineer based in NY, shares how building Gaia’s Follow Along mode — his first frontend project at Palantir — shifted his perspective on frontend engineering, while diving into the unique challenges of enabling real-time collaboration at scale.

Before joining Palantir, I thought frontend engineering was mostly about adding pixels, pushing them around, and making things look nice. While that’s certainly a component of frontend development, it’s nowhere close to the complete picture of what frontend engineering looks like here. At Palantir, frontend engineers are deeply involved in solving complex, novel problems that demand creativity, technical rigor, and close collaboration across teams.

My perspective didn’t change overnight — it changed through first-hand experience. Gaia Follow Along Mode was one of my first projects at Palantir, and it perfectly captured just how different frontend engineering is here.

Gaia Follow Along Mode

Palantir Gotham is Palantir’s platform for integrating, analyzing, and operationalizing complex data in mission-critical defense and intelligence environments. Used by American and allied forces worldwide, Gotham enables teams to collaborate seamlessly, share situational awareness, and make informed decisions — even in challenging operational contexts.

At the heart of Gotham’s geospatial capabilities is Gaia, our collaborative map application. Gaia enables teams to analyze and share geospatial data in real time, providing a common operating picture across distributed environments. The Follow Along feature in Gaia allows users to “follow” another user’s actions — tracking their cursor, zooming, panning, and selection activity as it happens.

This feature is particularly valuable in defense and other mission-critical environments, where teams are often distributed across remote bases and must operate under severe bandwidth constraints and high network latency. Traditional screen sharing is often impractical or even impossible in these settings; even when video teleconferencing is available, the resulting screen shares are low resolution or laggy. Operational users need a lightweight, reliable way to share situational context — one that doesn’t consume precious bandwidth, is resilient to latency, and doesn’t require high-end connectivity.

Follow Along is a feature that addresses the shortcomings of traditional screen sharing by transmitting only essential state (such as map position, cursor location, and other select information), and sending updates only as changes occur, rather than continuously streaming every frame of the screen. This approach enables real-time collaboration without the heavy network load of true screen sharing.

On the surface, it might look like a simple feature, but building it required thoughtful engineering across multiple dimensions:

Real-time collaboration: Developing a real-time collaborative feature introduced several unique challenges.

  • Shared state: We needed to reliably synchronize user actions across multiple clients, ensuring that every interaction was reflected almost instantly for all participants. To achieve this, Follow Along leverages an internal shared-state streaming framework, along with libraries such as Redux, to track and update specific map and selection properties in real time. Each client subscribes to updates for the relevant artifact, and only users with the appropriate permissions can participate.
  • Ordered updates: To guarantee consistency, we introduced a monotonically increasing update index for cursor events, ensuring updates are processed in order and preventing jumpy or inconsistent cursor movement for followers.
  • Follower chaining and control: We had to handle follower chaining and prevent circular follows (where users could end up following each other in a loop), and ensure seamless hand-offs when a follower wanted to take control.
  • Disconnection handling: We had to gracefully handle disconnections. For example, if the leader disconnected, the Follow Along session would automatically end for all followers. However, to account for poor network connectivity and intermittent disconnections, we implemented a timeout that waits 15 seconds after the leader disconnects before ending the session for the follower.

Performance: Our users are often deployed in austere environments, where bandwidth is low, latency is high, and compute and hardware resources are limited. To maintain a smooth and responsive experience, we made careful optimizations to minimize resource usage and maximize reliability.

  • Selective data streaming: Given the restrictive network bandwidth, we had to carefully scrutinize the data included in our updates. While our maps can support large-scale data, we intentionally designed the API to transmit only essential, lightweight information — such as user info, viewport, cursor location, and selection state — across the network.
  • Event throttling: We were selective not only about what data we sent, but also how frequently we sent it. For example, we processed only every third cursor event, reducing update frequency by two-thirds. This optimization helped maintain smooth cursor movement and minimized frequent re-renders that could degrade performance on devices with limited hardware, while also reducing the impact of network latency on the user experience.
  • Selective state synchronization: Updates are only stored and synced across clients when a user is actively being followed, to prevent unnecessary work and synchronization overhead — especially important in low-bandwidth environments.

Domains: Building for maps presented unique challenges that required domain-specific solutions.

  • Consistent cursor positioning: For example, we can’t rely on pixel coordinates to share cursor location because clients may have different screen sizes and aspect ratios. Instead, we use geo-coordinates (latitude and longitude) as the source of truth for the cursor position to ensure everyone saw the cursor in the correct location.
  • Contextual UI hiding: When in Follow Along mode, many map controls and accessory side panels are hidden for the follower. These are disabled to avoid distraction and to prevent accidental interaction by followers.
  • Viewport synchronization: We had to ensure that each follower was able to see the entire viewport of the leader. The leader’s viewport of the map can vary based on various factors, such as open panels, screen size, and aspect ratios. To achieve this, we introduced a bounding box that tracks the top-left and bottom-right geo-coordinates visible on the leader’s screen. For each follower, we would then scale and center their viewport to fit this bounding box, ensuring that the entire area visible to the leader was also visible to every follower, regardless of differences in device or screen size.
Example of viewport synchronization: the blue box on the right represents the leader’s visible map area. Both the leader’s (left) and follower’s (right) views are centered on the same geo-coordinate. Even though the follower’s visible view of the map differs from the leader, the follower’s viewport is scaled and adjusted to ensure the entire area visible to the leader is also visible to the follower.

In short, doing this kind of work meant building a deep understanding of both the tech stack — from React and Redux to internal frameworks for distributed state management — and domain-specific areas like geospatial rendering and real-time data streaming.

It also required developing a strong empathy for user pain points and the reality of how and where our products are used. We worked closely with designers and product managers to ensure the features built truly addressed real-world collaboration challenges.

An Unexpected Success Story

We built Gaia Follow Along mode as a bit of a bet — it wasn’t a feature users explicitly requested, instead, we engineered a solution based on the real pain points and feedback from operational users in the field. Initially, we enabled it at the request of a single user during a recent military exercise — almost as an experiment. To our surprise, it quickly became the #1 “tech win” of the event. Users found it incredibly impactful for secure, real-time collaboration on maps, and adoption spread rapidly as more teams discovered its value. The overwhelmingly positive feedback prompted us to share it across the company, and soon, other teams began to request demos and training.

Since then, Gaia Follow Along has evolved significantly, shaped by continuous user feedback from the field. We’ve added features like seamless hand-offs, allowing presenters to transfer their followers to another user, and customization options such as hiding usernames alongside the shared cursor. In subsequent projects, we made further optimizations. For example, some critical state is now passively streamed before a user starts following, ensuring that followers are immediately up-to-date when they join. Other state is only streamed once clients begin following, further reducing unnecessary data transmission. We have also scaled the system to support hundreds of concurrent users following the same leader, enabling large teams to collaborate in real time without sacrificing performance or reliability. Each new iteration was driven by feedback from people actually using the tool in high-stakes, collaborative environments. Each iteration required thoughtful engineering to meet evolving needs.

Example of a mock from a subsequent project to improve leader-follower hand-off and follow interactions. A great level of detail goes into each change and each small part of an overall feature.

Even though I no longer work directly on this feature, seeing it win the hearts of users and continue to evolve remains incredibly rewarding. It’s a testament to how frontend engineering at Palantir isn’t just about building user interfaces — it’s about delivering transformative experiences that truly matter to our users.

Gaia Follow Along mode is just one small glimpse into the vast landscape of frontend projects happening at scale across the company. If you’re passionate about building innovative and complex solutions from the ground up — solutions that have real-world impact — you’ll find no shortage of fascinating problems to tackle here at Palantir.

If this sounds like the kind of project and impact you’re interested in, check out our open roles today: https://www.palantir.com/careers/open-positions/. Our most applicable frontend postings are the “Web Application Developer” roles. We’re also hiring for these two specific roles right now: Software Engineer — Core Interfaces (Palo Alto), and Software Engineer — Defense Applications (DC).

Frontend Engineering at Palantir: Redefining Real-Time Map Collaboration was originally published in Palantir Blog on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

items.title: Frontend Engineering at Palantir: Drawing Circles on Maps
items.hover_description:
On building geospatial tools precise enough for polar operations and missile defense ranges.

About This Series
Frontend engineering at Palantir goes far beyond building standard web apps. Our engineers design interfaces for mission-critical decision-making, build operational applications that translate insight to action, and create systems that handle massive datasets — thinking not just about what the user needs, but what they need when the network is unreliable, the stakes are high, and the margin for error is zero.

This series pulls back the curtain on what that work really looks like: the technical problems we solve, the impact we have, and the approaches we take. Whether you’re just curious or exploring opportunities to join us, these posts offer an authentic look at life on our Frontend teams.

In this blog post, Nikita, a Frontend engineer based in DC, shares how rendering accurate circles on maps led him through map projections, spherical trigonometry, and the surprising complexity of visualizing ranges in polar regions.

A few months ago, a customer asked us to visualize the strike range of naval vessels operating in polar regions. Simple enough, right? Draw some circles on a map. Except when we tried the obvious approach, the circles looked like ellipses, cut off at weird angles, and sometimes wrapped around the world entirely. What should have been a simple feature turned into one of the more interesting frontend problems I’ve worked on at Palantir as a Frontend Engineer.

Why Circles Matter

Before we dive into the technical challenge, it’s worth understanding why this matters. At Palantir, we build software for people working on critical defense and intelligence problems with Palantir Gotham, our platform for integrating, analyzing and operationalizing the complex data their missions depend on. When these teams visualize geospatial data, accuracy is essential.

A circle on a map might represent:

  • The range of a missile defense system.
  • The coverage area of a cell tower network.
  • The blast radius of an explosive threat.
  • The operational range of a naval vessel.

If these visualizations are wrong, decisions get made with incorrect information. That’s not acceptable.

Map Visuals

In many development contexts, we leverage MapLibre, an open-source mapping library, to visualize geospatial data. To draw shapes — lines, polygons, points — we feed MapLibre geometries in GeoJSON format.

GeoJSON is perfect for web applications: it’s just JSON, so it works natively in JavaScript without conversion. It’s human-readable, lightweight, and the de facto standard for web mapping. MapLibre’s APIs are built around it. But the catch is, GeoJSON spec doesn’t include circles. The spec supports LineStrings, Polygons, Points, and various collections of these — but no circles.

This isn’t an oversight. Unlike polygons, which are defined purely by their coordinate vertices, circles require a radius — and that means choosing a unit. Should the radius be in meters? Miles? Degrees of latitude? Each choice leads to different results, and GeoJSON deliberately avoids encoding these kinds of measurement decisions into its geometry types. The spec sticks to coordinate-based shapes that work universally, leaving distance calculations and units to the application layer.

But there’s a deeper problem with circles on web maps, one that only becomes apparent when you try to implement them: map projections fundamentally distort what a “circle” even means.

Let’s Try Implementing

The naive solution is obvious: a circle is just a polygon with lots of points. Sample points around the circumference, connect them, and you’ve got yourself a circle.

Perfect! Well, almost — a sharp eye can see the individual sampled points and the straight lines connecting them. We can increase the sample rate to combat that. But for most purposes, this works great. Now let’s try the same technique with a radius of a few thousand miles.

Wait, what happened? The resulting shape looks like an ellipse on the flat map. But when we render the same points on a 3D globe, they form a perfect circle. This is where things get interesting. It is time we talk about map projections.

Map Projections

In cartography, a map projection attempts to represent the curved surface of a globe on a two-dimensional plane of a map. Here’s the fundamental issue: you cannot flatten a sphere onto a plane without distortion. All projections of a sphere on a plane necessarily distort the surface in some way. Every map you’ve ever seen is a compromise. All projections distort something — area, shape, distance, or direction.

Different projections make different trade-offs: Lambert Conformal Conic preserves angles for aeronautical charts but distorts areas; Albers Equal Area preserves area for thematic maps but warps shapes; Robinson splits the difference aesthetically but sacrifices accuracy entirely.

The most common projection is the Mercator projection. It’s the projection used by Google Maps, most GPS systems and many classroom maps. The Mercator projection became the dominant world map after its creation in 1569, because it’s exceptionally useful for navigation — any straight line on the map represents a constant compass bearing, making it simple for sailors to plot and follow courses. This practical advantage meant it remained the standard for centuries. As with other projections, the Mercator projection also distorts the true layout of Earth’s surface. It exaggerates areas far from the equator; the closer to Earth’s poles, the greater the distortion. One common example is that Greenland and Africa appear to be the same size, when in reality Africa is actually 14 times the size of Greenland.

There’s also an online tool that lets you see the real sizes of different countries: https://thetruesize.com/

Today, most online mapping services (including MapLibre) use Web Mercator, a modern variant optimized for digital maps. It’s computationally efficient and preserves local shapes well, which is why your neighborhood looks correct on Google Maps. But it still massively distorts areas near the poles. This is exactly the reason why our circle looks like an ellipse. At large scales, the projection’s distortion warps the visualization. The circle is correct on the sphere of Earth, but looks distorted on the flat map we’re rendering.

We’re Going to the Poles

This gets even worse for our Arctic naval operations customers. Some of their circles need to cross the North Pole itself. Let’s try to use our strategy of sampling and connecting points on the circumference to build a circle that includes the North pole (let’s also color the circle for visibility):

Oh no. The North Pole isn’t included in the resulting shape, the top is cut off, and the circle is repeating itself on the left and right edges of the map. Here’s what’s happening: the leftmost and rightmost points of our sampled circle shouldn’t be connected directly, rather they need to wrap around the world and connect with the copies of the circle on the copies of the map. This means that a circle crossing the North Pole in Mercator projection isn’t a closed polygon at all. It’s a sinusoidal line that wraps around the world. Let’s fix the geometries and see the result:

To verify that our approach is correct, let’s also visualize the same points on the globe.

Much better! The colored area now correctly represents the region within the circle’s radius, even though it looks nothing like a circle on the flat projection.

Exploring the Implementation

The real implementation is more complex than the high-level solution I described above. Let’s break it down into the key pieces: sampling points around the circumference, creating the circle outline and generating the colored fill.

Sampling Points Around the Circumference

First, we need a way to find a point given a center of a circle, radius, and bearing. This involves some spherical trigonometry (using haversine formula) that I will spare you the details of, but you can use open-source solutions like Turf.js’s destination function:

/**
 * Get the destination point from a given point, distance, and bearing.
 * Uses the haversine formula for calculations on a sphere.
 */
function destination(point, distance, bearing) {
 // Spherical trigonometry math goes here
}

Now, getting points around the circumference is straightforward: split 360 degrees into numPoints equal angles, and calculate the destination point at each bearing:

function getSampledCirclePoints(center, radius, numPoints) {
 const coordinates = [];
 
 for (let i = 0; i < numPoints; i++) {
 // It is -360 because we go in counterclockwise order
 // as per geojson polygon spec!
 const bearing = (i * -360) / numPoints;
 coordinates.push(
 destination(center, radius, bearing)
 );
 }
 
 return coordinates;
}

Handling the Circle Outline

Remember how circles crossing the poles aren’t closed polygons, but rather sinusoidal lines? This means we need to use GeoJSON’s LineString type instead of Polygon for the outline. The tricky part is finding the two coordinates that cut off the circle. This is when the line should cross the antimeridian (the International Date Line at 180 degrees longitude, which divides the planet into Eastern and Western hemispheres) instead. Here's the core logic:

function createPolarAwareCircleOutline(sampledPoints) {
 const lineCoordinates = [sampledPoints[0]];
 
 for (let i = 1; i < sampledPoints.length; i++) {
 const point = sampledPoints[i];
 const prevPoint = sampledPoints[i - 1];
 
 if (shouldCrossAntimeridian(point.lon, prevPoint.lon)) {
 // Adjust longitude to render on the next world copy
 const adjustedLon = point.lon + (point.lon < 0 ? 360 : -360);
 lineCoordinates.push([adjustedLon, point.lat]);
 } else {
 lineCoordinates.push([point.lon, point.lat]);
 }
 }
 
 return {
 type: "LineString",
 coordinates: lineCoordinates
 };
}
// If 2 points are more than half the world apart, we should cross the antimeridian!
function shouldCrossAntimeridian(lon1, lon2) {
 return Math.abs(lon1 - lon2) > 180;
}

The clever trick here is that MapLibre allows longitudes beyond the standard -180 to 180 degrees range. For example, a longitude of 200 degrees tells MapLibre to render the point on the next world copy to the east. This is how we make the circle wrap around correctly.

Handling the Colored Fill

The colored fill is trickier because it must be a closed polygon. If the circle includes a pole, we need to explicitly extend the polygon to that pole to ensure the fill covers the entire area. Depending on the way you sample the points, it will always be points at the same indexes which cross antimeridian. I will abstract finding these points in pseudocode because we also covered it above. Here’s how we handle pole-crossing circles:

function createPolarAwareCircleFill(sampledPoints) {
 let coordinates = [...sampledPoints];
 
 if (includesNorthPole) {
 // Get the point that should be across antimeridian
 const point = ...
 
 coordinates = [
 ...coordinates.slice(0, point_index),
 // Extend the polygon to the north pole
 [point.lon + 360, point.lat],
 [point.lon, 90],
 [point.lon + 360, 90],
 ...coordinates.slice(point_index),
 ];
 }
 
 if (includesSouthPole) {
 // Get the point that should be across antimeridian
 const point = ...
 
 coordinates = [
 ...coordinates.slice(0, point_index),
 // Extend the polygon to the north pole
 [point.lon, -90],
 [point.lon + 360, -90],
 [point.lon + 360, point.lat],
 ...coordinates.slice(point_index),
 ];
 }
 
 return {
 type: "Polygon",
 coordinates
 };
}

This gives us properly rendered circles at any latitude, any radius, even when they cross a pole or even multiple poles!

Why This Matters

What made this project particularly rewarding wasn’t just solving an interesting geometry problem — it was understanding the real-world stakes behind it. Our customers need accuracy at both the meter and the thousand-mile scale. They need it to work at the equator and around the poles. Understanding these requirements pushed me to solve the complete version of this problem, not just the simple “draw a circle on a map” version.

When we shipped this feature, analysts could finally visualize accurate threat ranges and operational areas in polar regions. They could overlay multiple circles, see intersections, and make confident assessments about coverage and vulnerability. This kind of precision matters when you’re supporting missions where getting things wrong isn’t an option.

If this sounds like the kind of project and impact you’re interested in, check out our open roles today: https://www.palantir.com/careers/open-positions/. Our most applicable frontend postings are the “Web Application Developer” roles. We’re also hiring for these two specific roles right now: Software Engineer — Core Interfaces (Palo Alto), and Software Engineer — Defense Applications (DC).

items.title: Better Living Through Github Bots
items.hover_description:
Editor’s Note: This is the third post in the Palantir Foundations series exploring how we customize infrastructure software for reliable operation at scale.

Palantir maintains approximately 6,000 repositories that touch production, spanning microservices, configuration-as-code, infrastructure-as-code, and other combinations. Each service owns its own repository, which teams independently operate. We refer to this layout as the “polyrepo.”

This architecture enables team autonomy, but it introduces a coordination problem when a developer needs to apply a cross-cutting change across thousands of repositories: a widely used dependency upgrade; a CI configuration change; or a wide migration. The cost scales linearly with the number of repos. The same class of problem appears in monorepos as they grow, though the failure modes differ.

The Developer Tools team and its parent Foundations organization are responsible for solving these cross-cutting problems. This post describes the GitHub applications we’ve built to do so.

Our Solution

Our approach is not a single tool or a platform rewrite. It is a set of focused GitHub applications, built incrementally over several years, that compose through GitHub’s native primitives of webhooks, status, checks, labels and pull requests.

Each application is independent and follows a Unix-like design philosophy: do one thing well. GitHub is the connective tissue between the workflows as bots subscribe to webhook events, evaluate conditions, and take action. Workflows are a side effect of these applications interacting through GitHub’s event system. Standardized build tasks and release processes across all repositories reduces overall frictions.

Core Applications

Policy-Bot
(open-source) — GitHub’s native branch protection rules support basic approval requirements, but lack the expressiveness needed for conditional policies at scale. Policy-bot enables complex, conditional PR approval rules beyond GitHub’s native options and supports path-based, author-based, and team-based predicates. Policies are defined declaratively in each repository or loaded from a shared remote configuration. Internally, policy-bot has evaluated 270k PRs across 4.5k repos in the last 30 days.

Bulldozer
(open-source) — Merging pull requests manually after all checks pass is a small but persistent source of latency and context-switching. Bulldozer subscribes to status and review webhook events and automatically merges pull requests once all required status checks pass and the configured merge criteria (typically the presence of a merge-when-ready label) are met. Bulldozer is stateless and evaluates merge eligibility on every event, taking no action until all conditions are satisfied. Bulldozer merged 250k PRs across 4.2k repos in 30 days.

Excavator
(internal) - A distributed system for applying changes across the polyrepo at scale. Authors define a program that runs in a sandboxed context against each target repository; Excavator executes it, computes the resulting diff, and opens a pull request. Use cases include dependency upgrades, CI configuration rollouts, and large-scale code refactoring. In the last 30 days, Excavator created or updated 300k pull requests across 5k repositories, running approximately 900 unique checks.

Label Maker
(internal) - Label Maker automatically adds labels to pull requests based on configurable predicates: changed file paths, PR author, base branch, and other conditions. Labels are triggers for other bots (like Bulldozer, Nit, and Autorelease), so automation can enable additional behavior on PRs rather than requiring a human to context switch between tasks. Label Maker added labels 235k times across 160k pull requests in the last 30 days.

Octo-Correct
(internal) - GitHub organization and repository settings are configurable through the UI, but manual changes are difficult to audit and easy to drift. Octo-Correct enforces repository and organization settings from a centralized declarative configuration stored in a single GitHub repository. It continuously reconciles actual state against desired state, reverting manual UI changes that fall outside the defined configuration. This provides a single point of visibility into all managed settings across the fleet. Octo-correct continuously managed 6200 repos in the last 30 days.

Nit
(internal) - CI failures caused by trivial issues such as lockfile inconsistencies and formatting violations create unnecessary review cycles. Nit subscribes to CI status events and, when it detects a class of failure it knows how to resolve, pushes a fix commit directly to the pull request branch. This keeps automated and human-authored PRs moving through the pipeline without requiring manual intervention for mechanical fixes. Nit has fixed 14k issues across 1k repos in the last 30 days.

Backport
(internal) - When a fix needs to land on older release branches, manually cherry-picking and resolving conflicts is error-prone. Backport automates this by replaying pull requests onto target branches in GitHub. Backport also integrates with Apollo release channels (https://www.palantir.com/docs/apollo/core/release-channels) to allow users to automatically select versions based on what is deployed to the field. Backport has created 3k backports across 200 repos in the last 30 days.

Autorelease
(internal) - Releasing software is often a chore and should not usually require human coordination. Autorelease monitors merged pull requests for the presence of a configured label (typically autorelease) and, when detected, creates a versioned release following our internal version schema. It supports multiple language ecosystems: Java, Go, Rust, Python, PNPM, and produces releases in a consistent, structured pattern. By supporting regular and non-toil releases, Autorelease promotes continuous release and deployment flows through Apollo (https://www.palantir.com/docs/apollo/core/products-releases-versions/). Autorelease has created 28k releases across 2k repos in the last 30 days.

Highline
(internal) - New repositories should start with current best practices by default, not accumulate them over time. Highline is a self-service application that provisions repositories from maintained templates, applying standard CI configuration, bot enrollment, and toolchain setup at creation time. Highline has created 100 repos in the last 30 days.

Go-Githubapp
(open-source) A Go library for building production-quality GitHub applications. It encapsulates common operational concerns: GitHub App authentication, installation token management, rate limit handling, and multi-organization operation. All of the above applications are built on go-githubapp.

Standardization

The applications described above are only useful at scale if repositories don't need to be configured individually. A system that requires each team to hand-author configuration for every bot in every repository would reintroduce the coordination overhead we set out to eliminate.

To solve this, all of our GitHub applications support remote configuration loading. Rather than reading configuration exclusively from the repository they're operating on, each bot can resolve its configuration from a shared source. We maintain a shared github org called standards that contains canonical, reusable configuration files for each application. When a bot evaluates a repository, it first checks for local overrides, then falls back to the appropriate configuration in standards.

Excavator then helps close the loop on application rollout. When a new bot or configuration is introduced, Excavator opens pull requests across target repositories to add the necessary local configuration or to migrate repositories to the standard remote configuration. Each new application benefits from the enrollment infrastructure that already exists, and each addition to standards increases the value of that shared configuration layer.

Composing Workflows — End to End Examples

Each application solves a discrete problem and they compound together. Consider the following change that resolves a CVE by upgrading a library and modifying code.

  1. PR Creation: Excavator runs continuously in the background and detects that new library version is available and opens a pull request on each affected repository. As part of PR creation, Excavator runs repository-local tooling to regenerate lockfiles (e.g., GCV for Gradle, go mod tidy for Go modules) so that the dependency graph is consistent at the point the PR is opened.
    When the pull request is opened, Label Maker evaluates the PR against its configured predicates and applies labels. Typically, merge-when-ready , autorelease, and fix nits. These labels will be used later on to trigger additional behavior.
  2. CI and Automated Remediation: GitHub triggers CI, which runs the repository’s test suite and reports back via status checks. If CI fails due to a mechanically fixable issue, such as a formatting issue or a lockfile inconsistency, then Nit detects the failure class from the CI provider and pushes a fix commit directly to the PR branch. This new commit triggers a new CI run. If CI fails for reasons Nit cannot resolve, the PR stalls and surfaces for human attention.
  3. Policy Evaluation: Policy-Bot evaluates the PR on each relevant event. For bot-authored PRs, policies are typically configured to approve without human review, conditional on predicates such as: the modified files fall within an expected set, the commit author matches the bot’s identity, and the commit is signed with a known key. If all predicates are satisfied, Policy-Bot sets its status check to success. Octo-Correct has already configured the required status checks for the repository from the centralized settings definition, ensuring that Policy-Bot’s check is among those required for merge.
  4. Merge: Bulldozer evaluates merge eligibility on every status event. Its conditions are: all required status checks passing, and the merge-when-ready label present. When both conditions are met, Bulldozer merges the PR. Bulldozer is stateless, so its evaluation is idempotent and it can safely process duplicate or redelivered webhooks without side effects.
  5. Release and Deployment: On merge, Autorelease detects the autorelease label and creates a versioned release following the internal version schema. The release is adjudicated through Apollo onto pre-stable development stacks. Vulnerability scanning then validates the product's CVEs and whether it can land on production stacks (see our previous blog post for details).

No human is required once the flow is set up. The dependency or change gets automatically updated, tested, checked for compliance, and deployed to the fleet.

Human-Authored Pull Requests

The event chain is identical with one key difference: Policy-Bot requires a human review.

When a developer opens a PR, Label Maker applies the same labels and CI runs the same checks. Nit will remediate mechanical failures, which are made by AI agents and humans more often than deterministic processes like Excavator. However, Policy-Bot’s predicates for human-authored PRs require at least one approving review from a teammate before setting its status to success. This is the gate that prevents auto-merge until a human has reviewed the change.

Once approved, the remainder of the flow is unchanged. Bulldozer merges, Autorelease cuts a release, and Apollo adjudicates deployment. If the change fixes a critical bug, the developer can invoke Backport to replay the PR onto older release branches, selecting target versions based on what Apollo reports as currently deployed to the fleet.

The bots handle the tedious work so developers can focus on what is interesting and hard.

Other applications can replace some of the above workflow, but the key principle is that each application can operate independently and do one thing right. For example, both dependabot and renovate are possible open source replacements for Excavator to open Pull Requests.

Automation Enables Failure At Scale

These workflows aren’t always perfect, and it is prudent to be thoughtful of the potential failure modes. For example, while backporting might seem like a simple operation against supported release branches, a developer once invoked backport on a monorepo across every version in the last year. The resulting load from CI saturation temporarily blocked other developers from testing their changes on different repos. The volume of large, uncached monorepo CI builds then saturated our artifact hosting, which further slowed builds and local development.

We added upper bounds on the number of PRs Backport can create in a single invocation. PR Rate limits are something we think about for other systems as well. Excavator applies similar constraints by default as it rate-limits PR creation to bound the load it places on GitHub’s webhook infrastructure.

Lessons Learned

We did not set out to build a developer platform. Each tool filled a specific gap, and the system grew incrementally around them.

Where possible, we’ve built stateless apps. Policy-Bot and Bulldozer are stateless, responding to GitHub webhooks. Excavator is smarter and needs state, but we accept that complexity for the value it provides.

We have learned the importance of measuring friction: Developer productivity is difficult to quantify reliably, even with frameworks such as SPACE<https://queue.acm.org/detail.cfm?id=3454124> and DORA<https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.5555/3235404>. Friction is more observable: where do developers file workaround scripts? Where do manual steps accumulate? Where do teams diverge from standard configuration?

We did not build these bots overnight, and no single bot was a massive step change on its own. We built Policy-Bot to improve GitHub reviews, Excavator to manage repos at scale, and Octo-correct to handle repo settings. The impact comes from sustained investment and the tools composing together. Over time, they’ve shifted the baseline so that developers spend less time on operational overhead.

Getting Started

PolicyBot and Bulldozer are open source. You can deploy them today:

  • PolicyBot on GitHub
  • Bulldozer on GitHub

Both run as stateless containers, respond to webhooks, and have no external dependencies. Start with one and see how it changes your workflow. Then consider what other gaps you could fill.

Better Living Through Github Bots was originally published in Palantir Blog on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.
